title: AI Agent的RAG、Memory底层的语义检索原理是啥 | 向量数据库-索引篇
text:
So, how does 'search by image' work?
Why can you just snap a pic in a shopping app
and find the exact same item?
And what's this 'facial recognition' black magic all about?
Behind them all lies
a frequently used technique in the AI world:
Vector Retrieval—or more precisely, vector retrieval
for massive amounts of data.
So, that begs the question:
what exactly are vectors?
And how is vector retrieval
for massive datasets even possible?
Today, we're going to connect all these dots
and break it all down.
By the end, not only will you get those questions answered,
but you'll also unlock the semantic retrieval principles
behind the hot topics
of RAG and Memory—key Agent technologies.
Like I always say, info online can be hit or miss,
so if there are any discrepancies,
just go with what I say.
So, before we start—did you hit that like button?
And follow? Thanks!
So, what's a vector? This is a cat,
and so is this one? And this one too?
This one ... uh, this isn't a cat.
Even though their styles are different,
you can always recognize them at a glance.
That's because your brain
is capturing multiple features at once,
like pointy ears,
a round face, and slender whiskers.
These features stack together
to form your overall impression of this image.
Now, the key word here is 'features.'
Computers can also use this approach—describing an object
with a set of features.
So, how do they do it?
Imagine a two dimensional coordinate system,
where the x axis represents whether the ears are pointy,
and the y axis represents whether there's a long tail.
A cat's image
would land in the upper right area of both axes,
but foxes also have pointy ears and long tails,
so in two D, they almost overlap.
Now, add a third dimension: 'is the face
round?' Cats have round faces,
while foxes have long, pointy ones,
so they get separated.
As the number of dimensions increases—say,
to one hundred and twenty eight—each dimension
corresponds to a specific visual feature.
Everything can find its own unique spot
within this multi dimensional coordinate system.
Different photos of the same cat,
even with varying angles and lighting,
will be positioned very close to each other.
The coordinates of each photo in this coordinate system
are a set of floating point numbers,
and this set of numbers is a vector.
Simply put, a vector is an array of floating point numbers,
which mathematically can be seen
as a point in high dimensional space.
The distance between vectors
represents how similar the original content is.
The closer the distance, the more similar the two images are.
By using the vector of one image
to find other images with nearby vectors from a larger set,
you achieve 'search by image'.
This is the same principle behind e commerce's '
'snap a pic to find similar items' feature.
You snap a photo with your phone,
it gets turned into a vector,
and then it searches the product database
for the product image vector
with the closest distance—that's your match.
Facial recognition works the same way:
a face photo is turned into a vector,
then compared against the face vectors
stored in a database—the face with the shortest distance
is the match.
Beyond images, text,
video, and audio—pretty much anything can be vectorized.
This enables all sorts of cool tricks,
like searching for images with text,
or searching for videos with images.
Whether it's image to image search or facial recognition,
what they're doing is essentially the same:
given one vector,
find the few vectors from a large set that are closest to it.
This problem of finding the nearest neighbor vector
from a large set of vectors
is known as the Nearest Neighbor Problem.
And this process of finding them
is called Nearest Neighbor Search.
So, what is HNSW?
And how do we implement Nearest Neighbor Search?
A straightforward idea is to take the input vector
and calculate its distance to every other vector, one by one,
then pick the closest one.
But for product or face databases,
there could be tens or even hundreds of millions
of vectors stored,
so iterating through all of them is just way too inefficient.
Scalars like numbers and strings can be quickly looked up
using indexes like the B+ tree,
without needing to iterate through everything.
But vectors are essentially arrays of floating point numbers,
which the B+ tree can't handle.
So, what kind of index should we use?
Well, there's a famous theory
called Six Degrees of Separation,
which states that any two people in the world
can be connected by at most six intermediaries.
Each vector is essentially a point in
multi dimensional Space,
just like a person.
We can take inspiration from social networks
and connect nearby points with edges
to form a neighbor graph.
When querying, you start from a certain point
and keep moving towards neighbors that are closer
in vector distance.
In theory, you should find the best match in just a few steps,
which means you don't have to traverse all the nodes.
But for Six Degrees of Separation,
you first need a solid starting point.
So, for such a massive graph,
where do you even start searching?
We can take inspiration
from the hierarchical structure of human society:
by layering,
we select a subset of nodes from the full, base level graph
to build a sparser, upper level graph.
Then, pick an even smaller set of nodes
to build another layer on top,
eventually forming a pyramid like, multi layered graph.
When a new vector comes in,
it starts from the single node on the top layer
and works its way down,
quickly pinpointing a general area within each layer.
Then, within these increasingly dense nodes,
it finds the nearest neighbor vectors
and establishes connections.
Querying for similar vectors follows the same process,
except that it returns the most similar results
from the bottom layer.
This multi layered graph index
is the renowned Hierarchical Navigable Small World,
or HNSW for short.
Enjoyed that?
So a Triple Combo wouldn't be too much to ask, right?
So, what's IVF?
Well, since HNSW only needs a few hops
to quickly find similar vectors,
it's super fast—but that speed comes at a clear cost.
The entire vector graph has to stay in memory,
so once the data gets big, memory becomes the bottleneck.
Is there a more memory friendly way?
Let's stick with the example of finding someone.
If you need to find someone in a white coat in a city,
you don't have to knock on every door;
you can just head straight to a hospital.
What you'd instinctively do
is sort people by their profession—doctors go to hospitals,
chefs to restaurants.
When searching for someone,
you first lock in on the category,
then search within it more closely.
Following this logic, we first classify these vectors,
grouping similar ones into the same 'bucket,'
where each bucket has a cluster center.
to represent the other vectors in that bucket.
So, when you run a query,
you first calculate the distance between your query vector
and all the cluster centers,
find the nearest buckets,
and then do a fine grained search within those buckets.
So, if you have ten million vectors
split into thousand buckets,
and you only search the ten closest buckets each time,
the number of candidates drops
from ten million
to one hundred thousand—cutting the computation
by ninety nine percent.
This initial coarse screening based on cluster centers
and then doing a fine grained search
within those bucket files—that's the Inverted File Index,
or IVF for short.
For those of you still awake and watching,
drop a 'zero' in the comments!
Let me see how many of you are still here.
So, what's Product Quantization?
IVF only stores the cluster centers
and the vectors within each bucket;
it doesn't need to maintain
all sorts of neighbor relationships
like HNSW,
so its memory footprint is smaller.
But for a one hundred and twenty eight dimensional
floating point vector,
each dimension is a float, which is four bytes,
so one hundred and twenty eight dimensions
make that five hundred and twelve bytes.
So, ten million vectors
would take up nearly five gigabytes of memory.
Plus, during queries, you have to calculate the distance
for every single vector in the bucket,
which is also very time consuming.
So, can we save even more?
Since IVF uses cluster centers
to represent an entire bucket of vectors,
let's take that idea a step further.
In a nutshell, it splits a vector into multiple sub vectors,
then uses a limited number of cluster center ID's
to approximate each of those sub vectors.
one hundred and twenty eight dimensions
is a bit too abstract.
To make it easier to grasp,
let's use four dimensional vectors
and replace floats with integers.
Let's say we have three vectors in our database
now. We'll split all four dimensional vectors
into two segments,
each sub vector being two dimensional,
and then perform clustering within each of these segments.
For example, for the first segment—meaning
the first two
dimensions—the cluster centers are these four points,
and for the
second segment—the last two dimensions—the cluster centers
are another four different points.
Each center is assigned a number,
and for each sub vector,
we find its nearest cluster center
and replace the original values with that center's number.
Take A for example: its first two dimensions are ,
which is closest to cluster center number two at ,
so we replace it with the number two.
Its last two dimensions are four to four,
which is closest to cluster center number three,
five to five,
so it gets replaced with number three.
The same applies to B and C.
In other words,
the vectors in the database are replaced, segment by segment,
with the ID of their nearest cluster center.
Note that what's being replaced is the ID number,
and as long as the number of clusters
doesn't exceed two fifty six,
a single byte is more than enough to represent it.
Originally, a four dimensional vector,
where each float thirty two takes up four bytes,
So, four dimensions would be sixteen bytes,
but now, just two ID's—meaning
two bytes—are enough to represent it.
That's an eight fold compression, saving a ton of memory.
Now, let's say a query vector Q comes in.
We also split it into two parts,
and for each part,
we calculate the squared distance
to the four cluster centers,
storing these values in a lookup table
like the one shown above.
Next, we can calculate its distance to vectors A, B, and C.
To find the approximate distance between q and A,
we use A's code to look up the table
and get a distance of twelve.
Likewise, the distance between q and B
is one hundred and thirty seven,
and between q and C, it's ninety seven.
This tells us that A is the closest,
and each data point only
requires two table lookups and one addition.
So for three vectors, that's six table lookups
and three additions,
for a total of nine operations.
In contrast, before compression,
each one required four subtractions,
four multiplications,
and three additions—eleven operations in total.
So for three vectors,
that's thirty three floating point operations—
a significant saving.
This method of saving memory and speeding up computations
through segmented vector quantization
is known as Product Quantization .
IVF narrows down the search scope.
Product Quantization compresses the memory and computation
for each vector.
Put them together, and you get IVF_PQ.
Approximate Nearest Neighbor.
Looking back, you've probably noticed that HNSW,
due to its graph structure,
might take a detour and miss the closest vector.
IVF: The target vector might land right on a bucket boundary
and get assigned to the neighboring bucket,
causing it to be missed.
Product Quantization : Replacing original values with ID's
inevitably leads to a loss of precision. Vector search,
unlike MYSQL's B+ tree, can't
pinpoint a specific row with exact precision.
This search method, which allows for a small margin of error
to find 'close enough' results, is called Approximate
Nearest Neighbor Search,
or ANN for short.
If you're still watching, drop a 'one' in the comments!
HNSW: it loads all vectors into memory,
prioritizing speed. IVF plus Product Quantization
trades some accuracy for space, reducing memory usage.
When you package these ANN indexing algorithms
into a database
that supports vector storage,
indexing, and retrieval,
you get a Vector Database.
Images, text, audio—any data
that can be converted into a vector
can be stored in it.
Using ANN indexing,
you can find the most similar results from tens of millions,
or even hundreds of millions of vectors, in milliseconds.
We used images as an example earlier,
but remember what we said at the start:
everything can be vectorized,
and that includes text.
So you ask AI, "What exactly is the Dark Forest Theory
from 'The Three Body Problem'?"
This sentence is turned into a vector by an encoding model,
which then retrieves the most relevant text
snippets from the knowledge base
and passes them to the large model to generate an answer.
This approach of first retrieving external data
and then feeding it to a large model to generate an answer
is called Retrieval Augmented Generation .
RAG Memory follows a similar logic:
it stores past conversations as vectors,
then when you chat next time,
it retrieves the most relevant memory snippets
and feeds them to the model,
so it can remember what you've said before.
So, the semantic retrieval behind RAG and Memory
is, at its core,
Vector Retrieval.
So, does that all make sense now?
Alright, if you found this video helpful,
be sure to share it with that one buddy of yours
who's still struggling.
The written notes are in the comments section.
This is Xiaobai Debug,
where we focus on technologies
that could shape human history.
If you're interested,
remember to follow us, and we'll see you next time!

# 向量检索与索引知识图谱

## 向量检索概览
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A1["输入（图像/文本/音频）"] --> A2["编码为向量（特征）"]
    A2 --> A3["高维向量空间"]
    A3 --> A4["计算向量间距离"]
    A4 --> A5["最近邻问题"]
    A5 --> A6["近似最近邻（ANN）"]
    A6 --> A7["索引结构（HNSW / IVF+PQ）"]
    A7 --> A8["检索最相似项"]
    A8 --> A9["应用（图像搜索、面部识别、RAG、记忆）"]
```

## HNSW 索引结构
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    B1["顶层节点（单一）"] --> B2["上层 2（更稀疏）"]
    B2 --> B3["上层 1（稀疏）"]
    B3 --> B4["底层基图（密集）"]
    B5["插入新向量"] --> B1
    B5 --> B2
    B5 --> B3
    B5 --> B4
    B6["查询向量"] --> B1
    B6 --> B2
    B6 --> B3
    B6 --> B4
    B7["贪婪遍历至更近邻居"] --> B4
    B8["在底层基图完成精确最近邻搜索"] --> B4
```

## IVF + 乘积量化（PQ）流程
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    C1["原始向量数据集"] --> C2["K‑means 聚类 → 桶中心"]
    C2 --> C3["倒排列表（Buckets）"]
    C3 --> C4["粗排：在桶中心计算距离"]
    C4 --> C5["乘积量化（PQ）"]
    C5 --> C6["每子向量的码本"]
    C6 --> C7["将向量编码为 PQ 码"]
    C7 --> C8["查表：子向量与码本距离"]
    C8 --> C9["细排：在候选桶内精细搜索"]
    C9 --> C10["返回近似最近邻结果"]
```

## RAG 与记忆检索流程
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    D1["用户查询（文本）"] --> D2["编码模型 → 查询向量"]
    D2 --> D3["向量数据库（ANN 索引）"]
    D3 --> D4["检索 Top‑k 记忆片段"]
    D4 --> D5["大语言模型（LLM）"]
    D5 --> D6["生成答案"]
    D6 --> D7["存储本轮对话向量"]
    D7 --> D8["记忆向量库（用于后续检索）"]
    D8 --> D3
```
